newsitem.title: INDIA: Wind of democracy blows through India's Congress.
newsitem.headline: Wind of democracy blows through India's Congress.

text.p: India's Congress party on Monday voted to choose a leader in a break with the traditional backroom dealing that epitomised the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty.

Sitaram Kesri, who assumed the party presidency last September when former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned in disgrace over a corruption scandal, was expected to cruise to victory in the three-man race to lead India's oldest party.
But the significance of the election lay as much in the whiff of democracy that it breathed into Congress's dealings as in the fate of the contenders.
"The Election Commission has put flabby politicos on a stern treadmill," the Times of India said.

It was the Election Commission that forced Congress's hand by recently announcing that it would recognise political parties only if they held democratic internal elections to choose new leaders by mid-June.
Congress, struggling to regroup after suffering its worst defeat in general elections last year, has held only three internal polls in 112 years.
It has ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947, with former prime ministers Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi in power for 37 of those years.

The commission's ruling, part of a broad drive to clean up Indian politics, has brought squabbling within Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party to a head as the group struggles to hold organisational polls by June 18.
Janata Dal's president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, has been linked to a fodder scandal, and the election has deepened a split within the party between his supporters and critics.
The results of the Congress polls were expected to be announced late on Thursday.
Kesri, who has had more than eight months to solidify his grip on the party, was tipped to win an easy majority among the more than 8,000 Congress delegates across the country.
Sharad Pawar, a former chief minister of Maharashtra state, and Rajesh Pilot, a former junior minister under Rao, were given little chance to upset the 76-year-old Kesri.
The Economic Times said "the ground appears set for a thumping win for Mr Sitaram Kesri".
Both Pawar, 56, and Pilot, 52, have tried to position themselves as youthful alternatives to the old guard within a party hobbled by corruption charges.

But Kesri was widely believed to be in a stronger position, which Pawar's backers attributed to the fact that, in a holdover from earlier days, most of the delegates where hand-picked by activists who in turn had been chosen by state leaders.
"We should be grateful for small beginnings and for this precedent, but the the process is still highly flawed," Vinod Mehta, editor of Outlook magazine, said.
All three Congress candidates said the rare electoral race would not lead to a split within Congress.

But Mehta predicted tension between Kesri and Pawar, who was expected to finish second, and said pressure would build on the former Maharashtra chief minister to step down as Congress leader in the lower house of parliament.
